description: EU regulation prohibiting market abuse including insider dealing, unlawful disclosure of inside information, and market manipulation. Replaces Market Abuse Directive (MAD). Applies to financial instruments admitted to trading on regulated markets, MTFs, and OTFs.

canonical_name: CSMAD — Directive 2014/57/EU on Criminal Sanctions for Market Abuse
description: Companion directive to MAR establishing minimum criminal sanctions for market abuse offences. Requires member states to criminalise: insider dealing, market manipulation, and unlawful disclosure. Minimum sentences: 4 years imprisonment for insider dealing and market manipulation.

MiCA Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 Art. 76-92 extends market abuse prohibitions (insider dealing, market manipulation, unlawful disclosure) to crypto-assets admitted to trading on crypto-asset trading platforms. Closely mirrors MAR framework.

Information of a precise nature, not publicly available, relating directly or indirectly to issuers or financial instruments, which if made public would likely have a significant effect on prices (price sensitivity test). Four cumulative conditions must be met.

Inside information in the context of US securities law terminology (equivalent to EU 'inside information'). Often used in AML typology descriptions. Possession of MNPI triggers restrictions on trading. MNPI misappropriation is both a MAR violation and a potential ML predicate.

Using inside information to acquire or dispose of financial instruments to which that information relates (dealing), recommending someone deal (recommending), or inducing someone to deal. Prohibition extends to tipping — communicating inside information to another person.

Actions creating false/misleading signals, securing abnormal prices, or employing fictitious devices. Includes: wash trading, spoofing, layering, pump-and-dump, painting the tape, front running, ramping. Must have capacity to affect price.

Buying and selling the same financial instrument simultaneously or in quick succession to create false impression of trading volume/price. Constitutes market manipulation under MAR. Also an AML red flag — may be used to establish artificial price basis or create transaction paper trail.

Placing orders with intent to cancel them before execution to create false impression of demand/supply and move prices. Constitutes market manipulation under MAR Art. 12. Also relevant in crypto markets under MiCA Art. 91.

Placing and cancelling multiple orders at various price levels to create an illusion of activity and manipulate prices. Closely related to spoofing. Used in algorithmic trading abuse. Prohibited under MAR. Also an AML typology name (separate meaning in ML context).

Artificially inflating the price of securities or crypto-assets through false/misleading statements (pumping) and then selling at inflated prices (dumping), leaving other investors with losses. Classic market manipulation scheme. Particularly prevalent in crypto and penny stocks.

Trading in financial instruments ahead of a large client order that will predictably move prices. Can constitute insider dealing (if using client order information as inside information) or market manipulation. Prohibited under MAR and MiFID II conduct of business rules.

canonical_name: MAR Art. 7 — Definition of Inside Information
description: Defines inside information: (1) precise nature; (2) not publicly available; (3) relates directly/indirectly to issuers or financial instruments; (4) price-sensitive (would likely have significant effect on prices if made public). Phased-in information also covered.

Market operators and investment firms must report suspicious transactions or orders to competent authorities when they reasonably suspect market abuse. Parallel to AML SAR obligation. STR filed with NCA (FI in Sweden, FIN-FSA in Finland). No tipping-off equivalent in MAR.

Issuers must disclose inside information as soon as possible via a regulated information disclosure system. May legitimately delay disclosure if: (1) immediate disclosure would harm legitimate interests; (2) delay not likely to mislead public; (3) confidentiality can be maintained.

canonical_name: AML SAR vs. MAR STR — Dual Reporting Obligation
description: Investment firms face dual reporting obligations: (1) AML SAR (AMLR Art. 69) — filed with FIU when ML/TF suspicion; (2) MAR STR (MAR Art. 16) — filed with NCA when market abuse suspicion. These are separate obligations with different triggers, recipients, and legal bases. Same transaction may trigger both.

canonical_name: MiCA Market Abuse Extension to Crypto
description: MiCA Art. 76-92 applies market abuse prohibitions to crypto-assets. Key extension: inside information concept for crypto (e.g., project developments, partnership announcements, liquidity events). Crypto trading platform operators have MAR-equivalent STR obligations. Creates first EU-level market abuse framework for crypto.

Investment firms subject to both MAR and AMLR have dual reporting obligations: MAR STR (market abuse suspicion → NCA) and AML SAR (ML/TF suspicion → FIU). Front running profits and pump-and-dump proceeds are ML predicate offences — market abuse generates ML risk. Both regimes must be satisfied.

MiCA Art. 76-92 creates a crypto-asset market abuse regime closely modelled on MAR. Key differences: no regulated market requirement (applies to any crypto trading platform), different inside information triggers, CASP reporting obligations. ESMA has issued guidance on application.

Process for investment firms to file MAR Art. 16 suspicious transaction reports: (1) Alert generated (TM system or analyst); (2) Analysis of whether transaction/order is suspicious re market abuse; (3) Escalation to compliance; (4) STR prepared using NCA template; (5) Filed electronically with NCA; (6) No tipping-off obligation (unlike AML).

Issuers must maintain a list of all persons who have access to inside information on a permanent or event-specific basis. Insider lists must be updated immediately. Submitted to competent authority upon request. Facilitates identification of potential insider dealing suspects.

Persons Discharging Managerial Responsibilities (PDMRs) and their closely associated persons must notify the issuer and competent authority of transactions in the issuer's financial instruments within 3 business days. Closed periods apply (30 days before results). Transparency measure.
